extracted.intended_audience: law and public-administration scholars, empirical researchers, and policymakers interested in measuring agency administrative/policymaking capacity
extracted.subtask_description: Constructing and validating quantitative measures of a federal agency's capacity to engage in policymaking using personnel records (OPM/EHRI/FedScope) and latent-variable modeling, with attention to task-specificity, component indicators, time-series comparability, and robustness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor measure to a specific task
rubrics_metrics.description: The measure must be tailored to a specific task; here, an appropriate measure of capacity would capture the agency’s ability to engage in policymaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design measures that align with the specific kind of work being assessed (e.g., policymaking vs. enforcement vs. adjudication); coding and indicator choices should reflect that task.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capture multiple components of capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: The measure must capture the various components of capacity; in policymaking, most capacity comes from the workforce’s ability to identify policy solutions and navigate process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include indicators for distinct theorized components (e.g., size, expertise, experience, team dynamics, and compensation) rather than relying on a single blunt proxy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enable time-series and cross-agency comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: An ideal measure will examine capacity over time across multiple agencies to allow for time-series comparisons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use longitudinal personnel data (multiple years) and consistent coding so researchers can observe changes and compare agencies across time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize bias and measurement error
rubrics_metrics.description: A valid measure should minimize sources of bias and reduce measurement error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer objective administrative data and standardized coding; be wary of sampling and response biases in surveys and of proxies that do not reflect substantive qualifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude non-policymaking employees
rubrics_metrics.description: Many EHRI employees do not engage in policymaking; excluding these employees (e.g., tax auditors, border patrol officers) helps reduce measurement error by tailoring the measure to policymaking tasks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and remove occupations unrelated to the targeted task to improve validity; document exclusions and test sensitivity to inclusion/exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use standardized occupational codes and OPM descriptions to identify policymakers
rubrics_metrics.description: Identifying employees engaged in policymaking is possible because the federal government uses a standardized set of occupational codes; reading OPM’s Handbook and position-classification descriptions to code occupations mentioning policymaking responsibilities is recommended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Code occupations as 'policymakers' when their OPM descriptions mention duties like 'developing regulations' or 'planning policies'; standardized codes improve comparability across agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include scientific/technical research occupations as relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: Include occupations described as conducting scientific or technical research, because individuals in these occupations often contribute to policymaking in more technical agencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test models with and without research occupations; the paper reports robustness (correlation ~0.80) when research occupations are included vs excluded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicator — Number of policymaking employees (workforce size)
rubrics_metrics.description: First indicator: the total number of policymakers within an agency constrains the amount of policymaking the agency can undertake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use counts derived from personnel records; recognize that size alone does not capture expertise or experience but is an important constraint on throughput.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicator — Proportion of policymakers with a college degree (substantive expertise)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure the substantive expertise within an agency’s policymaking workforce as the proportion of policymaking employees with a college degree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Education is used as a proxy for substantive expertise; include graduate-level education where appropriate and examine sensitivity to degree thresholds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicator — Mean length of service of policymakers (experience)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure the experience within the agency’s policymaking workforce as the mean length of service of policymaking employees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Length of service proxies accumulated procedural knowledge and professional judgment; compute averages by agency-year.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicator — Average salary of policymaking employees (compensation/retention)
rubrics_metrics.description: Include the average salary of the agency’s policymaking employees because recruiting and retaining expert and experienced policymakers depends in part on salaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust salaries for inflation and include locality pay adjustments to ensure comparability across years and locations; higher salaries are theorized to discourage exit and corruption and encourage performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicator — Proportion of white-collar workforce that are policymakers (organization/team dynamics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Include the proportion of the agency’s white-collar workforce comprised of policymaking employees as a proxy for organizational structure and team dynamics oriented toward policymaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This proportion is calculated by dividing the total number of agency policymakers by the total number of white-collar workers; use as an indicator of whether the agency is organized around policymaking tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggregate indicators with latent-variable modeling (Bayesian factor model)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aggregate the indicators into a single measure of capacity using latent-variable modeling (the paper uses a Bayesian factor model) because capacity is a latent trait not directly observed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Latent models let the data determine indicator weights rather than relying solely on researcher judgment; report model diagnostics, priors, and robustness to alternative specifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create agency-year scores and permit disaggregation by bureau
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct agency-year measures (scores) and where possible disaggregate to bureau-level scores depending on aggregation in OPM data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Produce time-series agency-year observations; disaggregate for large departments when OPM identifiers allow; report ranges, means, and SDs across agencies and years.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure baseline human capital only (scope limitation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The scores measure the baseline level of human capital within each agency and exclude external methods of augmenting capacity (e.g., detailees, contractors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge and discuss the implications of excluding detailees and contractors; these external sources shift or supplement capacity but require better data to incorporate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure capacity for policymaking tasks, not other agency functions
rubrics_metrics.description: The scores should be understood as measuring the ability of the agency’s workforce to complete policymaking tasks and are not designed to measure enforcement, litigation, adjudication, or benefits distribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If studying other tasks, develop task-specific indicators (e.g., fleet and location indicators for postal delivery) and code occupations relevant to those tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure prospective ability (potential) rather than observed output or workload
rubrics_metrics.description: Capacity is the prospective ability of an agency to complete a task; the scores measure potential for policymaking irrespective of how much policymaking the agency actually conducts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret high capacity even if observed policymaking is low (political choices may suppress activity); analyze capacity alongside observed outputs to understand use versus capability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not conflate capacity with workload — consider workload separately
rubrics_metrics.description: The scores do not incorporate a measure of agency workload; empiricists should evaluate relationships between capacity and policymaking in the context of agency workload.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where possible, include workload indicators in empirical models or at least discuss how workload might moderate capacity effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perform robustness checks and alternative specifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Scores should be tested for robustness to different configurations, alternative measures of the five indicators, and alternative subsets of occupations; compare against survey-based measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report sensitivity analyses (e.g., including/excluding research occupations, alternative education/experience measures) and correlations with other capacity proxies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use EHRI/FedScope personnel records as data source
rubrics_metrics.description: Leverage the Enterprise Human Resources Integration (EHRI) dataset (public version: FedScope) which contains individual-employee rows and characteristics like employer, occupation, education, salary, and length of service across years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine multiple years of EHRI to build time-series measures; document variable definitions and any data cleaning steps (e.g., excluding '-DEP' duplicates).

rubrics_metrics.name: Code policymaking occupations by reading position descriptions; provide examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Code occupations as policymakers by reading detailed occupational descriptions in OPM’s Handbook and including those that mention policymaking responsibilities; examples include attorneys, budget analysts, and foreign affairs specialists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide and publish the complete list of occupations coded as 'policymakers' and conduct appendix transparency showing coding decisions and lists (the paper references a complete list in its replication appendix).

rubrics_metrics.name: Standardized occupational codes improve measurement validity
rubrics_metrics.description: Using standardized occupational codes ensures that individuals in the same occupation perform similar tasks, have similar qualifications, and receive similar pay regardless of which agency employs them, improving measurement validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on OPM classification systems and document any recoding or mapping steps across years and classification systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let the data determine indicator weights via modeling
rubrics_metrics.description: A Bayesian/latent-variable model identifies which indicators best separate high-capacity from average agencies and affords higher weight to those indicators, instead of researcher subjective weighting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain the modeling approach, justify priors, and present how indicator loadings translate into the composite score.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perform standard data-cleaning (e.g., remove duplicate '-DEP' agency identifiers)
rubrics_metrics.description: When summing personnel counts for totals, exclude any agency identifier with '-DEP' in the name to avoid double-counting department-level aggregates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document cleaning rules and how totals were computed (the replication data explains summing TOTAL_RAWNUM and exclusion rules).

rubrics_metrics.name: Extend method to other tasks by recoding occupations and selecting relevant indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: The method can be extended to measure capacity for other tasks (e.g., adjudication) by coding occupations relevant to those tasks and constructing appropriate indicators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For non-policymaking tasks, select indicators tied to material resources or task-specific skills and validate the new latent construct separately.
